title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether computer-based scaffolding improves student learning outcomes in problem-based learning (PBL) for STEM education. The authors note that prior research had shown generally positive effects of computer-based scaffolding, but that traditional meta-analyses can be distorted by small-study effects and can struggle when few studies are available for particular moderator categories. To address this, they conduct a Bayesian meta-analysis of studies published from 1990 to 2015 that compare computer-based scaffolding with control conditions in PBL settings.

The intervention in this review is computer-based scaffolding, including conceptual, metacognitive, strategic, and motivational supports, and scaffold strategies such as feedback, question prompts, hints, expert modeling, and multiple strategies. The analysis also considers whether scaffolds were customized (fading, adding, fading/adding), how customization occurred (performance-adapted, fixed time interval, self-selected), what higher-order thinking skill was targeted (analysis, synthesis, evaluation), and the STEM discipline context. The review included 21 studies with 47 outcomes, all situated in STEM problem-based learning environments.

The meta-analysis found an overall positive effect of computer-based scaffolding on cognitive learning outcomes (g = 0.385), with effects varying by scaffold type and context. Metacognitive and strategic scaffolding showed larger effects than conceptual scaffolding; customized scaffolding, especially fading/adding, tended to outperform non-customized approaches; and self-selected customization methods showed the strongest effects among customization methods. Scaffolding was most effective for analysis-level outcomes and less effective for synthesis and evaluation, and effects were stronger in engineering, technology, and mathematics than in science or integrated STEM. The authors conclude that computer-based scaffolding is beneficial in PBL, but its impact depends strongly on design features and learning context.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a Bayesian meta-analysis with 21 studies and 47 outcomes, which is strong evidence synthesis. It uses explicit inclusion criteria, random-effects modeling, moderator analyses, and checks for small-study effects, though the authors note publication-bias concerns and heterogeneous priors.
impact_tier_rationale: The overall pooled effect is positive and small-to-moderate (g = 0.385), exceeding the threshold for medium impact. The findings suggest meaningful benefits for K-12 STEM problem-based learning, especially for analysis-level higher-order thinking.

interventions.use_case: computer-based scaffolding for K-12 STEM problem-based learning, including conceptual, metacognitive, strategic, and feedback/hint/question-prompt supports
intelligent tutoring system-style scaffolding discussed in the meta-analysis as a related computer-based support category, including adaptive hints and feedback in STEM learning

finding.finding_summary: Across 21 studies and 47 outcomes, computer-based scaffolding in STEM problem-based learning produced a significant positive effect on higher-order cognitive outcomes (g = 0.385, 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802). The review found the strongest gains for analysis (g = 0.537) and smaller gains for synthesis (g = 0.156) and evaluation (g = 0.147).
finding.measure: Higher-order cognitive outcomes / analysis, synthesis, and evaluation outcomes in STEM PBL
finding.effect_size: g=0.385 overall; g=0.537 analysis; g=0.156 synthesis; g=0.147 evaluation
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802 overall; analysis 0.038 to 0.981; synthesis 0.004 to 0.329; evaluation 0.003 to 0.288

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis focused on STEM problem-based learning and concluded that computer-based scaffolding improved cognitive learning outcomes in these science/engineering-oriented contexts, with an overall effect of g = 0.385. Effects varied by discipline, with science showing a smaller effect (g = 0.146) than engineering, technology, and mathematics.
finding.measure: Cognitive learning outcomes in STEM problem-based learning; discipline-specific subgroup effects
